title: Commas in compound and complex sentences
subject: LANGUAGE
skillNames: Commas in Compound Subjects and Predicates

slides.title: Two sentences, one comma
slides.text:
Two short sentences can be **joined** with **and**, **but** or **so**.

I was hungry. I ate a date.
→ I was hungry**, so** I ate a date.

slides.title: Comma before the joining word
slides.text:
Put the **comma before** and, but or so, not after it.

It was hot**, but** we played outside.

Not: It was hot but, we played outside.

slides.title: Check it
slides.text:
1. Find **and**, **but** or **so**.
2. Is there a full sentence **before** it and a full sentence **after** it?
3. If yes, put a comma **before** the joining word.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find the joining word: and, but or so.
2. Cover it. Is each side a full sentence?
3. If yes, there must be a comma before the joining word.

The sentence with a missing or misplaced comma is your proof.

sentences.t: The sun was out, so we went to the park.

example.explain:
**The sun was out** is a full sentence. **we went to the park** is a full sentence.

They are joined by **so**, so a comma goes **before so**.

together.passage: Nora has a little brother. He is three years old. She likes to read to him but he likes to run around. They have fun together.
together.stem: How should the third sentence be written?
options: She likes to read to him, but he likes to run around.
She likes to read to him but, he likes to run around.
She likes, to read to him but he likes to run around.
She likes to read to him but he likes, to run around.
together.hint: Find the joining word. The comma goes right before it, not after it.
together.good: Yes! Two full sentences are joined by but, so a comma goes before but.

sentences: She likes to read to him but he likes to run around.
evidence.stem: Tap the sentence that needs a comma.
evidence.wrong: This sentence is not two sentences joined together. Find the one with but.

checks.passage: It was raining, so we stayed inside.
checks.stem: Why is there a comma before so?
checks.why: It was raining and we stayed inside are both full sentences, joined by so.

checks.passage: I wanted to play ball but my friend was sick.
checks.why: The comma goes before but, so it comes right after ball.

checks.passage: Dad cooked rice, and Mom made salad.
checks.stem: Which word joins the two sentences?
checks.why: And joins Dad cooked rice and Mom made salad. The comma comes before it.

again.title: Two full sentences?
again.text:
Cover the joining word with your finger.

Can each side stand alone as a sentence? Then put a comma before the joining word.
again.example:
We were tired [so] we went to bed.

We were tired. ✓ We went to bed. ✓
→ **We were tired, so we went to bed.**

slides.title: Joining words
slides.text:
Seven short words can join two sentences: **for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so**.

Remember them as **FANBOYS**.

When one joins **two complete sentences**, put a comma before it.

slides.title: Two subjects: no comma
slides.text:
If **and** joins two **subjects** that share one verb, do **not** use a comma.

**Ali and Sami** played football.

Not: Ali, and Sami played football.

slides.title: Two verbs: no comma
slides.text:
If **and** joins two **actions** with the same subject, do **not** use a comma.

Huda **read a book and wrote a story**.

The second part (wrote a story) has no subject of its own, so it is not a full sentence.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find the joining word.
2. Look **after** it. Is there a **subject + verb** (a full sentence)?
3. Yes → comma before the joining word. No → no comma.

Point to the sentence where the comma breaks this rule.

sentences.t: Salma watered the plants, and her brother swept the yard.
Salma watered the plants and swept the yard.

example.explain:
In sentence 1, **her brother swept the yard** is a full sentence, so a comma comes before **and**.

In sentence 2, **swept the yard** has no subject, so there is **no** comma.

together.passage: On Friday, my family went camping in the desert. My father and my uncle set up the tent. My cousins collected sticks, and built a small fire. After dinner, we looked at the stars, and Grandpa told us old stories. It was the best night of the holiday.
together.hint: Look after each and. Is there a new subject, or just another action?
together.good: Yes! built a small fire has no subject of its own, so no comma is needed before and.

sentences: On Friday, my family went camping in the desert.
My father and my uncle set up the tent.
My cousins collected sticks, and built a small fire.
After dinner, we looked at the stars, and Grandpa told us old stories.
It was the best night of the holiday.
evidence.stem: Tap the sentence with the comma that should be removed.
evidence.wrong: The commas in this sentence are correct. After stars, Grandpa told us old stories is a full sentence.

checks.passage: Faisal and Majed walked to school together.
checks.stem: Why is there no comma before and?
checks.why: And joins two subjects, Faisal and Majed, who share one verb, walked.

checks.passage: The bell rang but nobody moved.
options: The bell rang but, nobody moved.
The bell, rang but nobody moved.
The bell rang, but nobody moved.
The bell rang but nobody, moved.
checks.why: The bell rang and nobody moved are full sentences, so a comma goes before but.

checks.passage: You can walk to the museum or you can take the bus.
checks.why: You can take the bus is a full sentence, so a comma goes before or.

again.title: Look for a new subject
again.text:
After the joining word, look for a **new subject**: I, he, she, we, they, a name...

**New subject + verb** → comma before the joining word.
**Just a verb** → no comma.
again.example:
Omar ran [and] he won. → new subject **he** → **Omar ran, and he won.**

Omar ran [and] won. → no new subject → **Omar ran and won.**

slides.title: Dependent clauses
slides.text:
A **dependent clause** has a subject and a verb, but it **cannot stand alone**. It starts with a word like **when, because, if, after, before, although, while, until**.

**When the rain stopped** ... (what happened?)

slides.title: Clause first? Use a comma
slides.text:
When a dependent clause comes **first**, put a comma after it.

**When the rain stopped,** we went outside.
**Because the road was closed,** the bus was late.

slides.title: Clause last? Usually no comma
slides.text:
When the dependent clause comes **after** the main clause, you usually do **not** need a comma.

We went outside **when the rain stopped**.
The bus was late **because the road was closed**.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find the word that starts a dependent clause (when, because, if, after...).
2. Is the clause at the **beginning** of the sentence? Find where it ends and check for a comma.
3. Is it at the **end**? Usually no comma.

Point to the sentence where the comma rule is broken.

sentences.t: Before the guests arrived, Mama arranged dates on a tray.
She made fresh coffee while we cleaned the room.

example.explain:
In sentence 1, **Before the guests arrived** comes first, so a comma follows it.

In sentence 2, **while we cleaned the room** comes last, so no comma is needed.

together.passage: Every year, our class visits the science center. When we arrived this year the guide gave each of us a map. We explored the space hall first because everyone wanted to see the planets. After we finished, we watched a short film about the moon. Although the day was long, nobody felt tired.
together.hint: Find a sentence that begins with when, after or although. Where does that first part end?
together.good: Yes! When we arrived this year is a dependent clause at the start, so a comma must follow it.

sentences: Every year, our class visits the science center.
When we arrived this year the guide gave each of us a map.
We explored the space hall first because everyone wanted to see the planets.
After we finished, we watched a short film about the moon.
Although the day was long, nobody felt tired.
evidence.stem: Tap the sentence with the missing comma.
evidence.wrong: This sentence is correct. Look for a dependent clause at the start with no comma after it.

checks.passage: If you finish early you can help me.
checks.why: If you finish early is a dependent clause at the start, so the comma comes after early.

checks.passage: We stayed inside, because it was too hot.
checks.why: The because clause comes after the main clause, so no comma is needed.

checks.passage: Although Badr was nervous he gave a great speech.
options: Although, Badr was nervous he gave a great speech.
Although Badr, was nervous he gave a great speech.
Although Badr was nervous, he gave a great speech.
Although Badr was nervous he gave, a great speech.
checks.why: The dependent clause Although Badr was nervous comes first, so a comma follows it.

again.title: Read it with a pause
again.text:
If the sentence starts with **when, if, because, after, before** or **although**, read it out loud.

You will hear a pause where the first part ends. Put the comma there.
again.example:
After we ate lunch (pause) we went home.

→ **After we ate lunch, we went home.**

slides.title: Comma splices
slides.text:
A comma **alone** cannot join two complete sentences. That mistake is a **comma splice**.

Wrong: The test was hard, we did well.

Fix it with a joining word (The test was hard**, but** we did well), a period, or a semicolon.

slides.title: However is not a joining word
slides.text:
Words like **however**, **therefore** and **then** cannot join sentences with just a comma.

Wrong: It rained, however we kept playing.
Right: It rained**;** however, we kept playing.
Right: It rained, **but** we kept playing.

slides.title: Test each part
slides.text:
Before you place a comma, test each part:

1. Two full sentences + a FANBOYS word → comma before the joining word.
2. One subject, two verbs → no comma.
3. Dependent clause first → comma after it.
4. Two full sentences + only a comma → comma splice. Fix it.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Split the sentence at every comma and joining word.
2. Label each part: full sentence, dependent clause, or verb phrase with no subject.
3. Apply the rule for that combination.

Point to the sentence where the parts and the punctuation do not match.

sentences.t: The museum opened at nine, but the line had formed an hour earlier.
Visitors waited patiently and talked quietly.
When the doors opened, everyone hurried inside.

example.explain:
Sentence 1: two full sentences + **but** → comma.
Sentence 2: one subject, two verbs → no comma.
Sentence 3: dependent clause first → comma after it.

together.passage: Coral reefs are some of the busiest places in the ocean. Thousands of species live among the corals and depend on them for food and shelter. When the water becomes too warm, corals can lose the tiny algae that live inside them. Without the algae, the corals turn white, this change is called bleaching. Scientists are working to protect reefs, and many divers volunteer to help them.
together.stem: Which revision fixes the error in the passage?
options: Without the algae, the corals turn white; this change is called bleaching.
Without the algae the corals turn white, this change is called bleaching.
Without the algae, the corals, turn white this change is called bleaching.
Without the algae, the corals turn white, and, this change is called bleaching.
together.hint: Find two complete sentences joined by only a comma. What can correctly join them?
together.good: Yes! The corals turn white and this change is called bleaching are both full sentences. A semicolon joins them correctly.

sentences: Coral reefs are some of the busiest places in the ocean.
Thousands of species live among the corals and depend on them for food and shelter.
When the water becomes too warm, corals can lose the tiny algae that live inside them.
Without the algae, the corals turn white, this change is called bleaching.
Scientists are working to protect reefs, and many divers volunteer to help them.
evidence.stem: Tap the sentence with the comma splice.
evidence.wrong: The commas in this sentence are correct. Look for two full sentences joined by only a comma.

checks.passage: The library was quiet, everyone was studying for exams.
checks.stem: What kind of error is this?
options: a missing comma in a list
checks.why: The library was quiet and everyone was studying for exams are full sentences joined by only a comma.

checks.passage: Our team practiced every day, however we lost the final match.
options: Our team practiced every day, however, we lost the final match.
Our team practiced every day however we lost, the final match.
Our team, practiced every day however we lost the final match.
Our team practiced every day; however, we lost the final match.
checks.why: However cannot join sentences with a comma. Use a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

checks.passage: The engineer checked the bridge, and wrote a report for the city.
options: A semicolon should replace the comma.
Remove the comma; the second part has no subject.
checks.why: Wrote a report has no subject of its own. One subject with two verbs needs no comma.

again.title: Label the parts
again.text:
Write a label over each part:

**S** = full sentence
**D** = dependent clause
**V** = verb with no subject

S + S with FANBOYS → comma. S + V → no comma. D first → comma. S, S with no joining word → fix it.
again.example:
The storm ended, the roads were wet.

S, S with no joining word → comma splice
→ **The storm ended, but the roads were wet.**
